Average House Prices by City with Top 10 Highlighted

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)  

# Summarize average price by city
average_price_by_city <- data %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(AveragePrice = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE))

# Summarize average price by ZIP code
average_price_by_zip <- data %>%
  group_by(statezip) %>%
  summarise(AveragePrice = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE))

# View the results
print(average_price_by_city)
## # A tibble: 44 × 2
##    city               AveragePrice

##  2 Auburn                  299340.
##  3 Beaux Arts Village      745000

##  7 Burien                  348947.

print(average_price_by_zip)

# Plot average price by city
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Rank cities by average price
average_price_by_city <- average_price_by_city %>%
  arrange(desc(AveragePrice)) %>%
  mutate(Top10 = ifelse(row_number() <= 10, "Top 10", "Other"))

# Plot average price by city with top 10 cities colored
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Convert average price to millions for plotting
average_price_by_city$AveragePrice <- average_price_by_city$AveragePrice / 1e6
overall_avg_price <- mean(average_price_by_city$AveragePrice)

# Plot average price by city with top 10 cities colored, and price in millions
ggplot(average_price_by_city, aes(x = reorder(city, AveragePrice), y = AveragePrice, fill = Top10)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_avg_price, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 1.0, 
             show.legend = TRUE, aes(label = "Overall Average")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(suffix = "M", prefix = "", scale = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Top 10" = "black", "Other" = "grey")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = "City", y = "Average Price (Millions USD)", title = "Average House Prices by City") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = "City Rank"))
## Warning: `geom_hline()`: Ignoring `mapping` because `yintercept` was provided.
## Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
## ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
## This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.

Note 1

Black Bars represent the cities that are among the top 10 in terms of average house price. These cities have the highest average prices in the data set. Gray bars: These represent all other cities in the data set that are not in the top 10 for average house prices. Red dashed line: This represents the average price of the overall housing.

From this graph, we can see that many cities have average house prices below the overall average, while only a few selected cities are substatially above this average. Cities significantly above the line, like Medina, Yarrow Point, and MErcert Island, are likely ot have unique attributes that drive higher prices, such as luxury amenities, waterfront access or the larger living spaces.

We can check what variables are most likely to affect the housing price so that we can give insights to prospective buyers.

Impact of Home Features on Price with Linear Regression

library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(caret)
## Loading required package: lattice
library(scales)

data <- data %>%
  mutate(bathrooms = as.numeric(bathrooms),
         bedrooms = as.numeric(bedrooms),
         sqft_living = as.numeric(sqft_living),
         sqft_lot = as.numeric(sqft_lot),
         floors = as.numeric(floors),
         waterfront = as.factor(waterfront),
         view = as.factor(view),
         condition = as.factor(condition))

# Splitting the dataset into training and testing sets
set.seed(123)  # for reproducibility
indexes <- createDataPartition(data$price, p=0.8, list=FALSE)
train <- data[indexes,]
test <- data[-indexes,]


# Fit the model
model <- lm(price ~ bedrooms + bathrooms + sqft_living + sqft_lot + floors + waterfront + view + condition, data=train)

# Get tidy summary of the model
tidy_model <- tidy(model)

format_millions_one_decimal <- function(x) {
  paste0(format(round(x / 1e6, 1), nsmall = 1), "M")
}

# Create a coefficient plot with 'M' formatted x-axis, one decimal place
plot <- ggplot(tidy_model, aes(x=estimate, y=reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype="dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = format_millions_one_decimal) +  # This formats the x-axis labels to millions with 'M'
  labs(y = "Variables", x = "Effect on Price (Coefficients)",
       title = "Impact of Various Features on House Prices",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line represents no effect") +
  theme_minimal()

# Add annotations for 'view' and 'condition' descriptions
plot <- plot + 
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = "view4", label = "View: 0 (No view) - 4 (Excellent view)", hjust = 1.1, vjust = 0, color = "blue", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = "condition5", label = "Condition: 1 (Poor) - 5 (Excellent)", hjust = 1.1, vjust = 0, color = "purple", size = 3)

# Print the plot
print(plot)

# Predictions and result dataframe
predictions <- predict(model, newdata=test)
result <- data.frame(Actual = test$price, Predicted = predictions)

# Output the first few rows of the result to see prediction performance
head(result)
##    Actual Predicted
## 1  313000  312762.6
## 4  420000  560920.7
## 7  335000  385634.4
## 8  482000  615680.5
## 19 257950  326905.9
## 22 435000  330995.3
# Load the necessary library
library(dplyr)

# Example of fitting a multiple regression model
model <- lm(price ~ waterfront + view + condition + bathrooms + floors + sqft_living + sqft_lot + bedrooms, data = data)

Note 2

This graph visually represents how difference house features affect the prices. For example, from this graph, we can see that house having waterfront has the most significant positive impact on house prices. Additionally, houses with better views generally increase in prie with better quality views. On the other hand, features like condition2, although positive, show very minor impacts compared to higher conditions, indicating diminishing returns or lesser valuation for moderate improvements in condition.

Mapping the Top Cities with High Housing Prices

#install.packages("ggplot2")
#install.packages("sf")
#install.packages("ggmap")

library(leaflet)
library(sf)
## Linking to GEOS 3.11.0, GDAL 3.5.3, PROJ 9.1.0; sf_use_s2() is TRUE
# Define data for the cities
top_cities <- data.frame(
  city = c("Newcastle", "Redmond", "Sammamish", "Fall City", "Beaux Arts Village",
           "Bellevue", "Mercer Island", "Yarrow Point", "Clyde Hill", "Medina"),
  latitude = c(47.5301, 47.6740, 47.6163, 47.5676, 47.5913,
               47.6101, 47.5707, 47.6209, 47.6309, 47.6205),
  longitude = c(-122.1635, -122.1215, -122.0338, -121.8887, -122.2009,
                -122.2015, -122.2338, -122.2330, -122.2196, -122.2364)
)

# Create the map
map <- leaflet(top_cities) %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addMarkers(~longitude, ~latitude, popup = ~city)

# Print the map
map

Note 3

This map clearly illustrates that the top 10 cities with the highest housing prices are located along the waterfront or near a lake. This suggests that homes in these areas likely have better views, contributing to their higher prices. Also, it’s clear that the areas with high housing prices are not scattered but are clustered together. This is important information for those looking to find the most affordable housing options. We can also see how other variables might affect the housing price.

# Plot with y-axis as integer for Price vs. Year Built
library(ggplot2)

# Plot with y-axis as price in millions for Price vs. Year Built
ggplot(high_cond_houses, aes(x = yr_built, y = price / 1e6)) +  # Convert price to millions
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(suffix = "M", prefix = "")) + 
  ggtitle("Price vs. Year Built for High-Condition Houses") +
  ylab("Price (USD)") +  
  xlab("Year Built") 
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Note 4

Each black dot represents a high-condition house. The x-axis indicates the year the house was built; the y-axis shows the price in millions of dollars. The blue line represents a linear regression, showing the general trend of house prices relative to their build year. The dashed area around the line represents the confidence interval for this trend.

From this observation, houses are spread across different years, with no particular concentration in any specific decade. Also, most high-condition houses are priced below $1 million, with a few outliers above $2 million and one above $3 million.

The slight downward slope of the line suggests a minor negative correlation between the year built and the price. This means that, on average, houses built earlier may tend to be slightly less expensive than newer houses, although the trend is not strong. In conclusion, the condition of a house is a significant factor, but this graph indicates that among high-condition houses, those built more recently tend to have higher prices. However, the correlation is weak, implying that other factors beyond the year built likely have a substantial impact on the price of high-condition houses.

The relationship between the living area square footage and the price of high-condition houses.

# Square footage and condition
library(ggplot2)

# Adjusting the plot to show price in millions
ggplot(high_cond_houses, aes(x = sqft_living, y = price / 1e6)) +  # Dividing price by 1 million
  geom_point() +  # Adds scatter plot points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +  # Adds a linear model line
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(suffix = "M", prefix = "")) +  # Formats y-axis labels in millions
  ggtitle("Price vs. Living Area Sq Ft for High-Condition Houses") +  # Adds a title
  ylab("Price (Millions USD)") 
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Note 5

This graph shows a positive correlation between the square footage of the living area and the price of high-conditioned houses. As the living area increases, the price of the houses also tends to increase, indicated by the upward slope of the blue line. This suggests that larger homes in good condition command higher prices. The shaded area around the line represents the confidence interval, showing the uncertainty or variability in the predictions. The data points are relatively well-clustered around the trend line, especially in the lower square footage range, indicating a consistent relationship across the dataset.

The relationship betwen square footage and price by renovation status (renovated vs. unrenovated)

data <- data %>%
  mutate(renovation_status = ifelse(yr_renovated == 0, "Unrenovated", "Renovated"))

# Summary statistics of price based on renovation status
price_comparison <- data %>%
  group_by(renovation_status) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median_Price = median(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    Count = n()
  )

# Output the results
print(price_comparison)
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   renovation_status Average_Price Median_Price Count
##   <chr>                     <dbl>        <dbl> <int>
## 1 Renovated               532441.       445000  1865
## 2 Unrenovated             565275.       480000  2735
library(dplyr)

# Adding a binary variable for renovation status
data <- data %>%
  mutate(is_renovated = ifelse(yr_renovated > 0, 1, 0))
lm_renovated <- lm(price ~ sqft_living, data = data, subset = is_renovated == 1)
lm_unrenovated <- lm(price ~ sqft_living, data = data, subset = is_renovated == 0)
library(ggplot2)

library(ggplot2)

# Plotting with enhanced visuals
library(ggplot2)

# Plotting with price in millions
ggplot(data, aes(x = sqft_living, y = price / 1e6, color = factor(is_renovated))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue"), 
                     labels = c("Unrenovated", "Renovated"),
                     name = "Renovation Status") +
  labs(
    title = "Price vs. Square Footage by Renovation Status",
    x = "Square Footage (sqft)",
    y = "Price (Millions $)",
    color = "Renovation Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14)
  )

Note 6

The red dots represent unrenovated houses, and the blue dots represent renovated houses. There is overlap in price cross many square footage ranges, telling that renovation status alone does not significanly affect to the price. Also, in both categories, there is an uupward trend, mening that if the square footage incereases, the prices also increase.

If renovation does typically result in a price premium, this could be a factor for homeowners to consider when deciding whether to renovate before selling. For buyers, it’s important to consider that while renovated homes might be more expensive, they could also offer better value through reduced need for immediate repairs or upgrades.

Comparing Actual and Prediced House Prices

# Plot Actual vs. Predicted Prices
format_millions <- function(x) {
  paste0(round(x / 1e6, 1), "M")  # Round to one decimal place and append 'M'
}

# Plot Actual vs. Predicted Prices with 'M' formatted labels
ggplot(result, aes(x=Actual, y=Predicted)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, color="red", linetype="dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = format_millions) +  # Apply custom formatting to x-axis
  scale_y_continuous(labels = format_millions) +  # Apply custom formatting to y-axis
  labs(x = "Actual Price (Millions)", y = "Predicted Price (Millions)",
       title = "Actual vs. Predicted House Prices",
       subtitle = "Red line represents perfect prediction") +
  theme_minimal()

Note 7

The graph shows how well a model can guess house prices. It does a great job predicting the prices of cheaper houses, up to about $1 million, because most of the dots are close to the line that shows perfect guesses. But for more expensive houses, above $1 million, the predictions aren’t as close. They start to spread out more and have bigger mistakes. This means the model might need some tweaks to better understand what makes those pricey houses special, or to fix any problems in the data it uses to make sure it’s more accurate for high-end homes.

Conclusion
